CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should maintain its retaliatory posture and signal willingness to negotiate from a position of strength, but avoid further unilateral escalation beyond matching US moves. We should continue diversifying trade partners and lowering tariffs on non-US goods to reduce dependency, while keeping the door open for talks after the US midterm elections.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not yet existential. The US has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese imports (roughly half of US-China trade), with threats to tariff the remaining $267 billion (Fox Business, Motley Fool transcript). China has retaliated covering $110 billion of $130 billion in US imports to China, meaning nearly all cards have been played on both sides. Soybean prices are down 20% (Brookings), and US farmers and manufacturers in specific sectors are feeling pain, but China's export economy faces real pressure from the tariff escalation. The Brookings analysis notes this is 'not a big hit for the overall U.S. economy' but will hurt specific sectors, suggesting the US has political room to sustain pressure through the midterms. China's retaliatory stance is justified because: (1) the US initiated the conflict and China must demonstrate it will not capitulate to trade bullying; (2) China has already lowered tariffs on goods from other countries to redirect trade away from the US, showing strategic sophistication; (3) the SCMP analysis suggests China is willing to buy more US products and open markets, indicating a negotiation path exists. However, further escalation beyond retaliation risks damaging China's own economy more severely, as China imports far less from the US ($130B) than it exports ($506B), limiting its retaliatory capacity. The optimal strategy is to hold firm, absorb short-term pain, and wait for post-midterm political dynamics to create space for a face-saving deal.
key_factors: US tariffs on $250B of Chinese imports (half of bilateral trade) with threats to cover remaining $267B
China has retaliated covering $110B of $130B in US imports - nearly exhausted retaliatory capacity
Soybean prices down 20% - US agricultural sector feeling pain from Chinese retaliation
No high-level negotiations scheduled; Trump admin views trade war as midterm election strategy
China lowering tariffs on non-US goods to redirect trade flows and reduce US dependency
Asymmetric trade volumes ($506B US imports from China vs $130B China imports from US) limit China's retaliatory options
SCMP reports China willing to buy more US products and open markets - negotiation pathway exists

The price of soybeans is already down 20 percent... This is not a big hit for the overall U.S. economy but it will hurt some specific sectors... the Trump administration will probably not change its strategy soon
China has stated that Washington is 'putting a knife to China's neck and that China will not participate in the trade bullyism of the United States'
China is willing to buy more products from the U.S. and open more markets, so their offer is clear
